# Commit Messages

The subject line says what the change accomplishes or prevents, in plain English. It is what a maintainer sees in `git log` and in release notes years later.

- Use the imperative mood and start with a capital letter: "Prevent", "Allow", "Keep", not "Prevented" or "Fixes".
- Keep it to 72 characters or fewer, with no trailing period.
- Do not use conventional-commit prefixes such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, or `refactor(scope):`.
- Do not name files, classes, or methods unless they are the point of the change. Describe the effect.
- An issue number alone is not a subject. Reference the issue in the body.

| Good | Bad |
| --- | --- |
| `Keep Func<T> working on Mono full AOT` | `fix: Func bug` |
| `Do not record a skipped conditional decorator as applied` | `Update DecoratorMiddleware.cs` |
| `Reduce allocations in child scope creation` | `perf(core): optimizations` |

Most commits need no body. Add one, after a blank line, when the reason or a trade-off is not obvious from the subject and the diff. Never retell the diff.

## Rules

- Do not add `Co-authored-by` or similar trailers naming an AI tool or model. The commit belongs to the person submitting it, who must be able to explain every line. Disclose AI assistance in the pull request description instead.
- If the repository has a `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, run `pre-commit run --all-files` and fix what it reports before committing. Do not skip hooks.
- Do not rewrite, amend, or force-push commits someone else may already have pulled unless you are asked to.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/commit.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/documentation.instructions.md -->
# Writing for People

Maintainers read every comment, issue, and pull request themselves, in their spare time. Writing that is twice as long as it needs to be gets read half as carefully. These rules apply to code comments, XML documentation, Markdown and reStructuredText, commit messages, issues, and pull request descriptions.

- Lead with why. The code shows what changed and how it works.
- Comment only where the reason for the code is not evident from the code: a constraint, a trade-off, an issue number for a regression test, or something a future reader might "fix" and break.
- Say each thing once. No summary that repeats the bullet list, and no closing paragraph that repeats the summary.
- Prefer a sentence to a paragraph, and a paragraph to a new section. A heading over two lines of text is not needed.
- Do not copy the code into prose. No lists of the files you changed, the methods you added, or the values you set. They go stale, and the diff already shows them.
- Point to things instead of repeating them: "the defaults are in `ContainerBuilderOptions`" rather than a table of every default.
- No preamble, no restating the request, and no wrap-up.
- Use US English spelling: behavior, color, canceled, initialize.

Brevity is not emptiness. XML documentation for public API still has to tell the reader something the member name does not: a parameter documented as "The index." helps nobody. Write the documentation you would want to read the first time you used the feature.

Length should follow how hard the change is. A subtle concurrency fix earns a longer explanation than a typo fix. Repetition never earns length.

Before presenting any of this writing, reread the draft against these rules and cut what they say to cut. A first draft almost always has something to remove.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/documentation.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/issues.instructions.md -->
# Issues

An issue is a request for a maintainer's time. Make it short, specific, and reproducible.

- File it in the repository that owns the code. Usage questions go to [Stack Overflow with the `autofac` tag](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/autofac), not to issues.
- Search existing issues, open and closed, before filing. Link a related one rather than repeating it.
- Follow the repository's issue template, and keep each section to what a maintainer needs.

## Bug Reports

- Give the smallest reproduction you can, ideally a failing xUnit test that uses only Autofac and the integration in question.
- Paste the full exception and stack trace as text, not a screenshot.
- List the versions of Autofac, the integration, and the .NET runtime.
- State what you expected and what happened, in a sentence each.

## Feature Requests

- Describe the problem you are trying to solve before the solution you want. A maintainer may know an existing way to do it.
- Show the API you have in mind with a short code sample.
- Say who else would benefit. Features are judged on how they serve Autofac users broadly and what they cost to maintain, following the library design rules.

Do not paste an AI-generated analysis of the codebase. If an AI tool helped you find the problem, confirm the problem yourself and report what you confirmed.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/issues.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/library-design.instructions.md -->
# Library Design

Applications we will never see depend on every public member, every default, and every behavior Autofac has shipped, including the accidental ones. Each decision below protects those users and the small group of maintainers who support them.

## The Public API Is Permanent

- Never remove, rename, retype, or move a public member, and never change its meaning. Removal takes a deprecation cycle: mark it `[Obsolete]` with guidance, keep it working, and remove it only in a major release.
- Source compatibility is not enough. The assemblies are strong-named, so a change that still compiles can still break an application at run time that was built against the previous version. Each of these breaks binary compatibility: adding an optional parameter to an existing method, changing a return type from `void`, moving an extension method to another static class, and changing a namespace.
- Adding a member to a public interface, or an abstract member to a public abstract class, breaks every implementer.
- A behavior change on an unchanged signature is also a breaking change. A different exception type, ordering, lifetime, or default breaks people as surely as a signature change does.
- Adding public API is a long-term commitment, not a convenience. Every new type, overload, or parameter needs tests, XML documentation, an entry in the documentation site, and support questions answered for years. Before adding one, show that the goal cannot be met with what is already public.
- Keep implementation details `internal`. Tests reach them through `InternalsVisibleTo`, which leaves room to refactor without breaking anyone.

When a change has to break compatibility, say so plainly in the pull request, and say why the break is worth it. Maintainers decide when a major version ships. Do not bump the version yourself.

## Make It Work, Don't Make It Optional

A new option, flag, or "opt-in" setting is usually a design decision that was put off. It moves the decision to every user, who knows less about the trade-off than the person writing the change, and it doubles the behavior that must be tested and supported.

- Find the design that is right for small and large applications alike. If a change helps large containers but costs small ones, keep looking for one that costs nobody, or show the cost is negligible.
- Do not gate a fix or an improvement behind a switch. If it is correct, it should be on for everyone. If it is not safe for everyone, it is not ready.
- When a setting genuinely cannot be avoided, the pull request must explain why no default works and what happens to people who never touch it.

## Run Everywhere Autofac Runs

Autofac targets old and new frameworks on purpose, so that taking an upgrade never forces anything else on an application.

- Respect each project's target frameworks. Core targets `netstandard2.0` through the newest .NET, and the classic integrations target .NET Framework. Code that compiles for only the newest target, or that behaves differently on an older one without a reason, is a defect.
- Core must stay compatible with trimming and Native AOT, and keep working on Mono and full AOT runtimes. Reflection or dynamic code generation needs an AOT-safe path or the correct trimming annotations.
- Never raise a minimum target framework or SDK requirement without a technical need for it.

## Performance Is a Trade-Off

Container code runs on every resolve in many applications, so allocations and time on the hot path matter. That is not a license for code nobody can maintain.

- Show the gain. A performance change comes with a BenchmarkDotNet run, in the repository's `bench` project if it has one, that compares against the current code and reports time and allocations.
- Weigh the gain against what it costs a maintainer to understand, debug, and safely change the code later. A small win that makes a core path hard to reason about is a loss.
- Optimize where the cost actually is: resolve paths, scope creation, and container build. Code that runs once per application gets clarity first.
- Do not trade correctness, thread safety, or platform reach for speed. Caches need a bound and a lifetime, and lock-free code needs to be correct under contention, not just fast without it.

## Dependencies Stay Minimal

- Core takes no third-party dependencies beyond the .NET base libraries.
- Do not raise a package reference's version without a technical reason: a needed API, a security fix, or a compatibility break. Every upgrade we take is one every consumer is forced to take. That includes integrations raising their minimum Autofac version.
- Any new dependency needs a license compatible with MIT, and the pull request must say why it is worth adding.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/library-design.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/project-context.instructions.md -->
# Autofac Project Context

Autofac is a dependency injection container for .NET with a history going back to 2007 and many millions of downloads. Most of its code was written by people, and people maintain it. Contributions are judged on how well they serve the users and the maintainers years from now, not on how much they change.

## Read Before Working

- `README.md` in the repository, and the [contributor guide](https://github.com/autofac/.github/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) shared by every Autofac repository. Where a repository has its own `CONTRIBUTING.md`, it adds to the shared guide.
- `.editorconfig`, `Directory.Build.props`, and the rulesets and `stylecop.json` under `build/`. Analyzers enforce these, and Release builds treat warnings as errors.
- `global.json` for the SDK, and `default.proj` for how the build runs. `dotnet msbuild ./default.proj` builds, tests, and packages most repositories.

## How the Repositories Fit Together

`autofac/Autofac` is the core container. Every other `Autofac.*` repository is an integration that depends on it, and some depend on each other, such as `Autofac.AspNetCore.Multitenant` on `Autofac.Multitenant`. A change to core can break integrations you are not looking at, and a change to an integration may need matching updates in [Documentation](https://github.com/autofac/Documentation) or [Examples](https://github.com/autofac/Examples).

File issues and pull requests in the repository that holds the code. A problem with the ASP.NET Core integration belongs in that repository, not in core.

## Workflow

- Libraries use Gitflow. Branch from `develop` and open pull requests against `develop`. Releases ship from `main`, and contributors never target it.
- Documentation, Examples, and this `.github` repository have no `develop` branch. Work against `main`.
- Behavior changes and new features start with an issue, so the design is agreed on before anyone writes code.
- Everything builds and tests with zero errors and zero warnings.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/project-context.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/pull-request.instructions.md -->
# Pull Requests

## Before Opening One

- Start from an issue for any behavior change or new feature, and wait until a maintainer agrees on the approach. A pull request that arrives with no issue risks rejection on design alone, however good the code is.
- Target `develop` in library repositories, and `main` in repositories that have no `develop` branch.
- Keep the change to one purpose. Do not bundle reformatting, renames, package upgrades, or "while I was here" fixes. Each of those is its own pull request, if it is wanted at all.
- Include tests that fail without the change and pass with it.
- Build and run the tests locally, with zero errors and zero warnings, before asking anyone to review.
- Review your own diff first. Remove debugging code, unrelated edits, and generated files that do not belong.

## Title and Description

The title becomes the commit subject when the pull request is squashed, so it follows the commit message rules.

The description tells a maintainer what problem this solves, how, and how you know it works. A maintainer should be able to read it in about a minute.

- Link the issue with `Fixes #123` or `Refs #123`.
- Say what changed in behavior, not which files changed.
- Call out anything a reviewer must not miss: a public API addition, a breaking change, a new dependency, or a behavior change for existing users.
- For a performance change, give one benchmark table comparing before and after, with time and allocations. Do not include every run.
- Leave out the implementation walkthrough, the list of tests you added, and test pass counts. The diff and CI show those.
- Use the repository's pull request template, and delete template sections that do not apply rather than filling them with "N/A".

## AI Assistance

If an AI tool wrote or substantially shaped the change, say so in the description, in one line. You are still the author. Read and understand every line before submitting, and be ready to explain and revise any of it yourself. Maintainers close pull requests whose submitter cannot.

## During Review

- When you address a comment, reply in a sentence with what you changed, or why you did not. A bare "done" adds nothing.
- Do not resolve a reviewer's thread. The reviewer resolves it once they agree it is fixed.
- Push related fixes together rather than one commit per comment.
- Do not rebase or force-push once review has started unless a maintainer asks.
- When commenting on someone else's pull request, make each comment one specific issue, question, or risk. Leave out praise padding, restated code, and your reasoning steps.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/pull-request.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/csharp.instructions.md -->
# C# in Autofac

These rules are the standard even where existing code disagrees. Much of the code predates them, so nearby code is not evidence of a convention. Where these rules and the analyzer configuration are silent, match the surrounding code, and say which you did.

## Source

- Start every file with the copyright header from `build/stylecop.json`. StyleCop reports a missing or altered one.
- Use file-scoped namespaces that follow the folder path.
- Name private and internal fields `_camelCase`, and constants and `static readonly` fields `PascalCase`. Locals and parameters are `camelCase` with no prefix.
- Put user-facing exception and diagnostic messages in the `.resx` file next to the class, such as `ContainerBuilderResources.resx` beside `ContainerBuilder.cs`, and format them with `string.Format(CultureInfo.CurrentCulture, ...)`. Do not inline message strings.
- Validate public arguments with `throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(x))` and the like. `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` does not exist on `netstandard2.0`.
- Use the newest language features the project's `LangVersion` allows, but no API missing from one of its target frameworks unless it is behind `#if` with an equivalent fallback. Build every target before submitting.
- Use `ConfigureAwait(false)` on every `await` in library code. Never block on async work with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
- Assume concurrent use. Containers and lifetime scopes are resolved from many threads at once, so shared state needs a clear synchronization story, and that story belongs in a comment.
- Do not add reflection, `Expression.Compile`, or `MakeGenericType` without an AOT-safe path, or without the `[RequiresUnreferencedCode]` and `[RequiresDynamicCode]` annotations the trimming analyzers ask for.
- Catch only exceptions the code can handle or must wrap. The resolve pipeline catches broadly to wrap activation failures in `DependencyResolutionException`, which is an existing boundary, not a pattern to copy elsewhere.

## Analyzer Warnings

Fix the warning instead of suppressing it. A warning that looks wrong usually keys on something cheap to change. Suppress only after showing that the rule does not apply here and no reasonable change satisfies it, and ask the maintainers first. Use `[SuppressMessage]` with a `Justification` on the narrowest member, never project-wide `NoWarn` or a `GlobalSuppressions.cs` file. Test projects may set `NoWarn` for `CS1591` (missing XML documentation).

## XML Documentation

Every public and protected member has XML documentation, because it becomes IntelliSense and the API reference.

- `<summary>` says what the member is for, in terms the name does not already give.
- Document each `<param>`, `<typeparam>`, and `<returns>`, and add `<exception>` for exceptions a caller can anticipate and handle.
- Use `<remarks>` for usage guidance, lifetime or threading behavior, and anything surprising.
- Use `<see cref="..."/>` to link types and members rather than naming them in plain text.

## Tests

- Use xUnit. Use NSubstitute for new mocks, but do not change an existing test project's mocking library. Prefer a real or hand-written implementation to a mock when it is simple to build.
- Autofac has two kinds of test, each in its own project. Choose by what the test exercises, and name it to match. Older tests mix the two and use other names. Leave them alone unless you are already rewriting them.
  - **Unit tests** check how one type does its job: argument validation, internal behavior, and members an application does not call in normal use. A test is a unit test even when it calls public API, such as checking that `Register` rejects a null delegate. They go in a project named after the project they test with a `.Test` suffix, such as `Autofac.Test`, in the folder matching the type's source folder.
  - **Specification tests** check what an application can count on when it uses a feature: what it gets back, and the failures it can anticipate and handle, such as resolving a service that is not registered. They go in a project with a `.Specification.Test` suffix, such as `Autofac.Specification.Test`. No `InternalsVisibleTo` names it, so the compiler holds these tests to the public API.
  - When a test fits both, ask whether it checks a failure the caller handles or misuse the caller fixes. Misuse, such as a null argument, is a unit test. Everything else an application observes through the public API is a specification test, even when one member does the resolving.
- Name a unit test class after the type it tests with a `Tests` suffix, `ContainerBuilderTests`, and keep every test for that type in it. A static class with many extension methods, such as core's `RegistrationExtensions`, may have one class per member instead: `RegistrationExtensionsRegisterDecoratorTests`. Name each method `MethodName_StateUnderTest`, where the second part is the input or state and never the outcome: `Register_NullDelegate`, not `Register_NullDelegateThrows`. Constructor tests are `Ctor_StateUnderTest`.
- Name a specification test class after the feature with a `Tests` suffix, `KeyedServiceTests`, and each method after the behavior it pins down, as a PascalCase phrase with no underscores: `ResolveIEnumerableReturnsEveryRegistration`.
- A bug reported from application code gets a specification test that reproduces the report. Specification tests are the contract, so changing what one asserts is a behavior change, and the pull request must say so.
- An integration that implements another framework's contract runs that framework's conformance suite, such as `DependencyInjectionSpecificationTests`, by inheriting it in the `.Specification.Test` project.
- Keep tests in each class in alphabetical order.
- Make each test self-contained: build what it needs in the test body or through a static helper, not through shared fields or constructor setup.
- Every test asserts something. To show no exception is thrown, assert that `Record.Exception` returns `null`. To show an exception is thrown, use `Assert.Throws<T>`, never `try`/`catch`.
- Write one test per invalid argument rather than one parameterized test. Assert the exception type only, not its message or parameter name.
- Do not add Arrange, Act, and Assert comments.
- A bug fix includes a regression test that fails without the fix. Mention the issue number in a comment on the test.

# Markdown

Markdown here must pass markdownlint with the repository's `.markdownlint.json`. pre-commit runs it. These rules cover what the linter cannot check.

## Structure

- Use one `#` heading as the document title, and nest headings in order without skipping a level.
- Write headings in Title Case. Do not use bold text in place of a heading.
- Do not create a sub-heading with no siblings, or a list with only one item. Fold it into the text above.
- Put introductory text directly under the title rather than in an "Overview" section.

## Formatting

- Never hard-wrap prose. Each paragraph and each list item is one line, however long.
- Use `-` for bullets and `1.` for numbered lists, and indent nested lists to the parent item's text.
- Give every fenced code block a language, such as `csharp`, `xml`, `powershell`, or `text`.
- Put code, type names, file paths, and commands in backticks.
- Avoid raw HTML. GitHub renders Markdown, and HTML makes the source harder to read.

## Content

- Link text must make sense out of context. Link the words "contributor guide", never the word "here". Do not leave bare URLs in prose.
- Give every image alt text that describes what it shows.
- Write short sentences in the active voice, with common words.
- Start each list item with a capital letter.
- Use emoji rarely, never as list markers, and never as the only way something is said.
- Write "ID", not "Id" or "id", in prose, and write "and" rather than "&".
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/markdown.instructions.md -->

<!-- Source: .github/instructions/powershell.instructions.md -->
# PowerShell

Scripts here run on Windows, macOS, and Linux under PowerShell 7, in CI and on contributor machines, and nobody is around to answer prompts.

## Style

- Name functions and scripts with an approved verb from `Get-Verb` and a singular noun: `Update-AiInstruction`, not `Do-Updates`.
- Use full cmdlet and parameter names. No aliases such as `%`, `?`, `ls`, or `gci`, and no positional parameters except the first argument of a well-known cmdlet.
- Name parameters in `PascalCase` and locals in `camelCase`. Reuse common parameter names such as `Path`, `LiteralPath`, `Force`, and `PassThru` when they mean what the built-in cmdlets mean.
- Build paths with `Join-Path`, never by concatenating strings with `/` or `\`.
- Indent four spaces, with opening braces on the same line.

## Behavior

- Start scripts with `[CmdletBinding()]` and a `param()` block, and use `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest`.
- Take all input through parameters. Never call `Read-Host` or otherwise prompt.
- Add `SupportsShouldProcess` to anything that changes files, repositories, or remote state, and call `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess()` right before each change so `-WhatIf` works. Pushing, opening pull requests, and publishing happen only behind an explicit switch.
- Use `-ErrorAction Stop` on calls whose failure must stop the script. Check `$LASTEXITCODE` after every native command, such as `git`, `dotnet`, or `gh`, because PowerShell does not stop on their failure.
- Write data to the output stream as objects. Use `Write-Verbose` for progress, `Write-Warning` for problems, and `Write-Error` or `throw` for failures. Reserve `Write-Host` for interactive summaries.
- Restore any global state you change, such as the current location or an environment variable, in a `finally` block.
- Exit with a nonzero code when anything required fails.

## Help and Checks

- Give every script and exported function comment-based help with `.SYNOPSIS`, `.DESCRIPTION`, every `.PARAMETER`, and at least one `.EXAMPLE`.
- Run PSScriptAnalyzer with the repository's settings file if it has one, and fix what it reports rather than suppressing it.
- Test with Pester 5 where a script has logic worth testing.
<!-- End source: .github/instructions/powershell.instructions.md -->

# GitHub Actions

Library repositories do not define their own build. Each one has a `.github/workflows/main.yml` that calls the shared `autofac/.github/.github/workflows/ci.yml@main` with `secrets: inherit`, passing only the inputs that differ from the defaults. Fix build behavior in the shared workflow, not by adding steps to one repository.

- A change to the shared workflow runs in every library repository on its next build. Keep inputs backward compatible: add new inputs with defaults, and never rename or remove one that a `main.yml` passes.
- The shared workflow stays self-contained. Inside a reusable workflow, `uses: ./...` resolves against the calling repository, so it cannot call sibling workflows in `autofac/.github`.
- Pass untrusted event data, such as titles, branch names, and bodies, through `env:` rather than interpolating `${{ github.event.* }}` into a `run:` script.
- Give each job the narrowest `permissions:` it needs.
- Comment the reason for anything that is not obvious, such as an event filter, a concurrency group, or a skipped job.
